messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Stan 3 density notation: final stages
parts:
I updated with respect to the Stan meeting discussion on Tuesday:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments

I think we're nearing agreement. To summarize, the unnormalized
form is:

target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);

and the normalized form is

target += normal_lpdf<norm>(y | mu, sigma);

We add = for assignment and deprecate <- and support += generally, but
only allow target to be used on LHS with +=.

We change suffix _lp to _target and _log to _lpdf in user-defined functions.

We do not allow vectorization control (at least for now).

We do not add a special link=logit, etc. form of control.

All existing functionality still supported, but deprecated. If we get
it in before Stan 3, we could just pull it out from under people in
Stan 3, or we could wait a year. The downside is all the material written
using our existing notation; the risk is that people will keep using
the existing notation, even if we deprecate it.

There are still a couple issues to resolve:

* vertical bar with lcdfs, lccdfs, and ldiff_cdfs?

* allow access to target as a value?

* allow vectors on RHS of += the way we do with increment_log_prob()?

Anyway, none of this will be at all challenging to build, though there's
going to have be a ton of tests around it to make sure it all works
and the deprecation warnings are right.

- Bob

seen!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f

On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 1:06:32 PM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
I'm curious to see what users' reactions will be when we change assignment from "<-" to "=" given that the majority of users seem to use the RStan interface and are used to "<-". Personally, I'm fine with making that change, as it brings Stan more in line with the overwhelming majority of programming languages, but I do think there is something nice about using "<-" for assignment, as "=" already has other uses unrelated to assignment.

If we do += for incrementing target, then it makes sense to use = for assignment. And it would be pretty easy for the parser to catch a <- and suggest changing it to =. And it is pretty easy for people to do a find-and-replace in their existing Stan programs. But it is a change that affects almost every line without providing a whole lot of benefit. Perhaps if there were more people in favor of the @ notation, we could keep <- for assignment.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 3 density notation: final stages
parts:
What we're really defnining as a model with a Stan
program is often the joint density of a combination of
discrete and continuous variables.

No no no no no no no.  I know Andrew likes thinking about
models this way due to the prior/likelihood ambiguities in  
hierarchical models, but that’s not what we do in Stan.

Stan defines a conditional probability density function,
p(alpha | beta) where alpha are defined in the parameters
block (or functions there of) and beta are defined in data,
transformed data, or sometimes as local constants.  The
importance of this distinction, besides where the variables
are defined, is that alpha must be continuous while beta 
can be continuous or discrete.

Sloppy equivalences like

p(alpha | beta) \propto p(alpha, beta)

make sense only when we keep this type distinction in
mind and can actually drop the intermediate constant.  
If we were just defining a joint distribution then we could 
write

p(alpha, beta) = p(alpha | beta) p(beta) \propto p(beta | alpha)
p(alpha, beta) = p(beta | alpha) p(alpha) \propto p(alpha | beta)

hence p(beta | alpha) and p(alpha | beta) would be
equivalent!  But Stan can define the only the latter
when any of the beta are discrete.

To be more formal, what we are defining is a disintegration of
the joint distribution p(alpha, beta) which requires more
information than the joint distribution itself.

target = log p(theta | x) + Z(x)

written and include the normalization terms, what you
get for lp__ (target) is log p(theta, x), not
log p(theta | x).

But what's cool about Stan is that you don't have to
code the model that way. As long as whatever you code
is proportional to p(theta | x), you're good to go.

parts:
It'll work just like any other program, like

double f(double x, sigma) {
double target = 0;
target += -(x * x) / (sigma * sigma * 2);
target -= log(sigma);
return target;
}

A variable is part of the function definition. Given
an execution context and state of execution (for
instance, called with x = -1.2, sigma = 0.5,
done executing first two statements), it will have
a value. So in a progamming language context, you
usually think of a variable as a mapping from
execution contexts (often modeled as some kind of
continuation) and a value. The value will have a type
determined by the variable's type.

will underlying be an accumulator collecting a sequence
of values (usually autodiff variables) and will itself
have to be evaluated to get a result (the evaluation is
just summing, but we collect them up for efficiency to
reduce the size of the resulting expression graph). Another
difference is that it's implicitly declared and initialized
(optionally) to the Jacobian of the constraining transform.

I originally derived "lp__" from "log pdf" and "log pmf"
because Andrew calls pdfs and pmfs "probability functions"
in BDA and "lp__" was the internal accumulator for the log
probability function. In retrospect, I regret that decision
because it's too easy to take it to mean "log probability", and
it's a density, not a probability.

The reason I don't like the unmarked case "normal(y | mu, sigma)"
for the log density is that I want the expression to just be a function,
and the function normal( | , ) is pretty much universally understood
in papers and textbooks to mean the linear scale.

I don't mind "lognormal_log", but "poisson_log_log" is pushing
things. I also don't like neg_binomial_2, becuase like the link=log,
it's just another parameterization (though I don't think it's
considered a link function when you switch normal or gamma or negative
binomial parameterizations).

- Bob

P.S. Why is "pdf" lower-cased? It's not pronounced like
a word, so even Andrew wouldn't lower-case it on
first principles. Maybe the early probability theory
authors thought "PDF" everywhere looked tacky :-)

This is exactly why being explicit is important — when everything is properly
labeled the Stan program itself can put errors into context.  You can’t have
pmfs with parameters left of the bar, or CDFs incremented into the target,
etc, etc.  Also the names give users something to look up when they’re
running into trouble.  All of this needs to be supported in the doc, but it
leads to a much cleaner user experience, especially for new users (it’s
always better to have a giant pile of material to read than not know what
your problem is).

Again, I’m not arguing for what is easier for _me_ to read/use, but rather
new users.
